item.title: My First Job as a Junior Developer
item.summary: A young developer in Tashkent looks back on his first months at work, a serious mistake and what his mentor taught him.
item.content_markdown:
Six months ago, I started my first job as a junior developer at a small software company in Tashkent. I had studied programming online for two years, and I thought I was ready. I wasn't, at least not completely.

In my first week, I was given a simple task: fix a bug on the login page of a delivery app. I found the problem quickly and felt very proud. But I didn't test my change properly, and when it went live, nobody on Android could log in for almost an hour. I wanted to disappear.

My team lead, Dilshod, called me into a meeting room. I was sure he was going to fire me. Instead, he asked me to explain exactly what had happened. Then he said something I have never forgotten: "Everyone breaks something in their first month. The important thing is what you learn from it." Together, we wrote a checklist that I still use before every update.

Since then, Dilshod has become my mentor. Every Friday, we spend thirty minutes looking at my code. He doesn't just tell me what is wrong; he asks questions until I find the answer myself. It's slower, but I remember the lessons much better.

If I could give one piece of advice to new developers, it would be this: don't be afraid to ask questions. In my first weeks, I wasted hours because I didn't want to look stupid. Now I know that a good team would rather answer ten questions than fix one big mistake.
